title: Lobbyists vs Patients
narration_text: Always. Ten lobbyists who each make ten million dollars from war will outfight ten million patients who each lose ten dollars from disease.
context: A stark mathematical comparison between the power of concentrated war lobbying and diffuse health interests.

title: Real Economics
narration_text: This is mathematically correct and morally disgusting, which is how you know it's real economics.
context: The narrator critiques the cynical but accurate reality of modern economic incentives.

title: Profitable Inefficiency
narration_text: The current system persists not despite its inefficiency but because of it. Inefficiency is profitable for the people running it.
context: Highlighting that the current system's failure is actually a source of profit for those in power.

title: The Coordination Problem
narration_text: The part Olson didn't account for: the people getting screwed have ninety times more money. They just can't coordinate.
context: Pointing out that the collective victims of the system have more total capital but lack a way to act together.

title: Concentrated Market Cap
narration_text: Concentrated interests like defense and fossil fuels represent approximately five trillion dollars in market cap,
context: Estimating the total market value of the sectors currently dominating political spending.

title: Political Spending Disparity
narration_text: with current political spending between one hundred million and one billion dollars annually.
context: A look at the specific dollar amounts spent on political influence by established industries.

title: Potential Wealth vs Cures
narration_text: Diffuse beneficiaries, meaning everyone who would benefit from cures, represent four hundred and fifty-four trillion dollars in household wealth,
context: Contrasting the wealth of established industries with the vast collective wealth of the global population.

title: Coordination Failure
narration_text:
but their current political spending is approximately zero due to coordination failure.

Having more capital doesn't help if you can't deploy it.
context: Explaining why massive collective wealth fails to influence policy without a coordination mechanism.

title: Deploying Capital
narration_text: That's Olson's whole point and he's right. A ninety to one capital advantage means nothing when each individual's share is too small to motivate action.
context: Discussing how small individual stakes prevent large groups from acting on their collective financial advantage.

title: Incentive Alignment Bonds
narration_text:
Coordination costs eat everything.

Incentive Alignment Bonds are a coordination mechanism disguised as a financial product.
context: Introducing Incentive Alignment Bonds as the tool designed to solve the coordination cost problem.

title: Investing in Change
narration_text: They turn political change into an investment. Investors don't need to care about curing disease. They need to care about returns.
context: Explaining how I.A.B.s shift the motivation for social good from altruism to profit-seeking.

title: Curing Disease for Returns
narration_text: The returns happen to require curing disease. Whether this actually works at scale is an open question (nobody's tried it),
context: The narrator acknowledges the experimental nature of using financial returns to drive medical breakthroughs.

title: Lobbying for Health
narration_text: but the logic is: if you can make "lobby for health" pay better than "lobby for war," lobbyists will lobby for health.
context: Summarizing the logic of using financial incentives to steer lobbyists toward beneficial social outcomes.

title: A New Cascade
narration_text:
This is not a controversial claim about human nature.

Why the cascade can happen (not "must" happen).
context: Setting the stage for how the I.A.B. cascade might unfold in reality.

title: Concentrated Benefits
narration_text:
Once I.A.B.s concentrate financial benefits on the pro-health side:

Politicians face a new calculation:
context: Showing how I.A.B.s change the political math by centralizing the rewards for health policies.

title: Policy Funding Strength
narration_text:
I.A.B. benefits are greater than concentrated opposition costs.

Each policy success increases I.A.B. funding, which strengthens the coalition.
context: How success in the I.A.B. system creates a self-reinforcing loop of more funding and stronger support.

title: Treaty Expansion Return
narration_text:
Investors lobby for treaty expansion to increase their returns.

The dynamic reverses: supporting clinical trial funding becomes the concentrated-benefit option.
context: Describing the final stage of the cascade where supporting trials becomes the most profitable path for investors.

title: Funding and Opposition
narration_text: This isn't inevitable. It requires sufficient I.A.B. funding to overcome opposition, and "sufficient" is a number nobody can calculate in advance.
context: Acknowledging that the success of this plan depends on reaching a tipping point of funding.

title: The Ratchet Effect
narration_text:
But the capital exists. It just needs a reason to move.

Why This Scales: The Ratchet Effect.
context: Transitioning to the 'Ratchet Effect' as the mechanism that allows the system to scale upward.

title: Expansion Incentives
narration_text: Each treaty expansion creates more political incentive funding to lobby for the next expansion.
context: Explaining how the financial structure of the treaty encourages continuous growth and expansion.

title: One Percent Funding
narration_text: At one percent, political incentive funding is two point seven two billion dollars per year.
context: Providing concrete numbers for the political influence generated even at low levels of reallocation.

title: Reward for Politicians
narration_text: At ten percent, that scales to ten times as much. Politicians who supported the one percent treaty get rewarded.
context: Describing how the rewards for participating politicians grow as the reallocation percentage increases.

title: Direction of Progress
narration_text:
Those rewards grow if they push for two percent.

It's a ratchet that only moves in one direction: the direction where people stop dying.
context: Characterizing the system as a one-way mechanism toward progress and life.

title: Historical Ratchets
narration_text: You've accidentally built ratchets like this before (Social Security, Medicare), but always by accident and never on purpose.
context: Noting that humanity has created similar permanent systems before, though not with deliberate foresight.

title: Wishonian Example
narration_text:
This time, try doing it on purpose.

On Wishonia, we built this ratchet four thousand two hundred and ninety-seven years ago.
context: The narrator reveals that the alien planet Wishonia successfully implemented this long ago.

title: A Three-Decade Pivot
narration_text: It took us about three decades to go from one percent to full reallocation, which felt slow at the time
context: Reflecting on the timeline it took for Wishonia to fully transition their global economy.

title: Efficiency of Reallocation
narration_text: but looks quite efficient compared to your six thousand years of not trying.
context: A final sharp comparison between Wishonia's progress and Earth's lack thereof.
